summary: Changes one rule of the IETF Nominating Committee process in RFC 3777 so the committee may publish the list of nominees who are willing to serve. This allows community members to give feedback about candidates. It is a Best Current Practice, and it was replaced by RFC 7437.

eli5.summary: A group picking leaders used to keep the list of volunteers secret. This rule lets them show the list to everyone, so people can say what they think of each volunteer before the choice is made.

questions: can the nomcom publish the list of nominees
how does the nominating committee select leaders
subtitle: Allows the IETF Nominating Committee to disclose the list of volunteers willing to serve in leadership positions.

tldr.problem: The IETF Nominating Committee (NomCom) needed community feedback on leadership candidates, but confidentiality rules made it hard to solicit input widely. The existing practice of sending shortlists to select groups wasted community effort and left some people out.
tldr.mechanism: This update to RFC 3777 allows NomCom to publish the full list of nominees who are willing to serve, without disclosing which ones are the top contenders. The community can then give feedback on all willing candidates.
tldr.outcome: The change enables broader participation in the nomination process and more balanced feedback, while keeping final deliberations confidential.

today: RFC 7437 obsoletes this document with additional clarifications to the NomCom process. The open disclosure of willing nominees is now standard practice in IETF leadership selection.

sections.title: Why Transparency Helps
sections.content:
The Nominating and Recall Committee (NomCom) selects leaders for the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG), the Internet Architecture Board (IAB), and IETF administrative positions. RFC 3777 requires that NomCom deliberations and nominee information remain confidential.

However, NomCom members do not personally know all the candidates for every position, so they need feedback from the broader IETF community. Past NomComs quietly sent shortlists to hundreds of selected experts—working group chairs, area directors, document authors—but this practice violated the strict confidentiality rule and excluded many community members who could have provided useful input.
sections.eli5: A committee needs to know what people think of volunteer leaders. They used to secretly ask a few experts, but that wasn't fair to everyone else and was against the rules anyway.

sections.title: The Old Problem and New Solution
sections.content:
The old practice had two problems. First, it was not official, so conscientious committee members worried about breaking confidentiality rules. Second, because some nominees on the shortlist were 'padding' (not real candidates), the community wasted time giving feedback on people who had already declined. Also, the secrecy meant some IETF participants had no way to know who was being considered and could not offer relevant input.

This RFC changes the rule explicitly: NomCom may now publish the list of willing nominees—people who have said they are open to being considered. By disclosing only willing nominees and not the real vs. padding distinction, NomCom can solicit feedback from the entire community without wasting effort on people who declined and without needing to secretly break confidentiality rules.
sections.eli5: Instead of secretly asking a few people, they can now openly say 'here are the people who said yes to being considered' and ask everyone what they think. That's fair and wastes less time.

sections.title: How Disclosure Works
sections.content:
NomCom discloses the list of willing nominees for each position. Committee members can ask the entire IETF community for feedback on those candidates. The published list contains only names of willing nominees; it does not identify who is on the shortlist for serious consideration, preserving some confidentiality of deliberations.

NomCom may choose which willing nominees to include in the disclosed list and may update the list if the committee identifies errors or receives new willing nominees partway through the process. Nominees themselves should not lobby publicly for support, and the community should provide feedback to NomCom rather than making public endorsements or criticisms.
sections.eli5: NomCom says 'here are the volunteers we're looking at' and asks everyone to comment. They don't say who their top picks are. People should tell the committee privately what they think, not argue on the mailing list.

sections.title: Status and Context
sections.content:
This document is a Best Current Practice and updates RFC 3777, the definitive NomCom process document. The change reflects what leading NomComs were already doing unofficially, making the practice explicit and adding structure to prevent abuse. The RFC acknowledges concerns that nominees might be reluctant if their names are public or that published lists might invite unwanted lobbying, but concludes that broad, transparent feedback outweighs these risks.

RFC 7437 later obsoletes this document with further refinements to the NomCom process.
sections.eli5: This is official guidance, and a newer RFC later updated it with more improvements.
